newsitem.title: HONG KONG: More records tipped for HK stocks.
newsitem.headline: More records tipped for HK stocks.

text.p: Hong Kong's record-breaking stock market is expected to achieve further highs in the coming week, taking its lead from the Dow's bull-run, brokers said.
"The market is likely to follow the Dow to a new high next week," said Francis Wu, institutional sales manager at South China Securities.
"But if the Dow corrects, so will Hong Kong. Technically, the Hong Kong market is very overbought," Wu said.
The Hang Seng Index powered ahead 73.25 points to a record high close of 12,510.05 on Friday. Over the week, the index put on a total of 291.65 points, a gain of 2.4 percent.

The market's strong end-week run ahead of a three-day weekend, with a local holiday on Monday, capped a record-breaking week. The Hang Seng Index closed at record highs on Monday and Tuesday, and set an intra-day high of 12,602.34 on Wednesday.
Adding to the impetus provided by the Dow's advance was HSBC Holdings run-up, which has led the market for most of the year, brokers said.

"I think HSBC will continue to lead the market significantly higher...essentially it (the share price) is only now in the middle of what we consider to be fair value for HSBC, said Carlton Poon, director and head of Hong Kong research at Worldsec International.

The banking giant, which accounts for 18 percent of the blue chip index capitalisation, added HK$2.00 (US$0.26) to close at $155.00 on Friday, after touching a new high of HK$155.50 earlier in the day.
While the bulls are upbeat, they may now be hedging their bets a bit.
"Yes, the market is expensive by some measures. For example, the PE (price/earnings ratio) of the market now is at the high end of its trading range of the last 10 years, said Poon.
"But if you take a longer perspective, the P/E of the market has been higher, much higher, he said.
"For the last 10 years, in particular, we have had a political discount in Hong Kong, and relative to that political discount (due to the 1997 handover) the market is high."
The British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
"The easy gains are over," said Chris Roberts, regional technical strategist at HSBC James Capel.
Roberts said the market was a bit vulnerable to any short-term weakness, and if the index broke below the previous day's low, this would signal a more significant fall of 200 points to 300 points.
